article_title: The Role of Selective High Schools in Equalizing Educational Outcomes
citation: Allensworth, E., Moore, P., Sartain, L., & de la Torre, M. (2016). The Educational Benefits of Attending Higher-Performing Schools: Evidence from Chicago High Schools. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications
title: Four-tier classification of Chicago high schools by graduation rate and average ACT score
description: The research groups Chicago high schools into four performance tiers using graduation rate and average ACT composite score: selective enrollment, top-tier non-selective, mid-tier non-selective, and low-tier non-selective. Figure 1 prints, for the CPS Class of 2015, a "90.0" four-year graduation rate and "24.5" average ACT for the 10 selective schools, versus "50.6" and "14.8" for the 28 low-tier schools. This tiering is the basis for all outcome comparisons in the summary.
requirements: Schools are classified by graduation rates and ACT scores, with non-selective tiers defined relative to average ACT scores and graduation rates
constraints: Non-selective tiers include neighborhood, charter, and special high schools, so tier differences are not purely selectivity differences
target_learners: first-time ninth-graders in Chicago Public Schools
target_learning_goals: high school achievement, student experiences, and college outcomes
examples: Figure 1 reports the CPS Class of 2015 average performance by tier, e.g., top-tier schools with an 82.3 graduation rate and 18.5 average ACT
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Moore, P., Sartain, L., & de la Torre, M. (2016). The Educational Benefits of Attending Higher-Performing Schools: Evidence from Chicago High Schools. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications

article_title: The Landscape of Career Readiness Opportunities in Chicago Public Schools
citation: Illinois Workforce and Education Research Collaborative (IWERC), in partnership with the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. (2024). The Landscape of Career Readiness Opportunities in Chicago Public Schools: Strengthening Career and Technical Education and Establishing Career-Connected Learning for All. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Career-connected learning (CCL) as a districtwide framework unifying college prep and career readiness
description: The report describes CPS's vision and enactment of "career-connected learning" (CCL), a framework initiated in 2017, which aims to unify college preparatory and career readiness activities districtwide. The framework operates through two strategies: strengthening existing high school CTE programs and establishing a districtwide CCL framework for students from grades 6 through 12. Chicago is presented as one of many districts working to implement a modern CCL framework.
requirements: District-level coordination of existing initiatives and systems across decentralized schools
constraints: CPS is decentralized, so network and school leaders make program decisions, and funding for new initiatives is limited
target_learners: High school students in Chicago Public Schools
examples: District leaders focused on strengthening CTE programs of study and unifying initiatives through Learn.Plan.Succeed.
key_sources: Illinois Workforce and Education Research Collaborative (IWERC), in partnership with the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. (2024). The Landscape of Career Readiness Opportunities in Chicago Public Schools: Strengthening Career and Technical Education and Establishing Career-Connected Learning for All. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Predicting Student Attrition in Competitive Programming: A Large-Scale Study Integrating Survey Insights and Global Behavioral Logs
citation: Azuad Islam Ruhan, Golam Mostofa Naeem, Rakibul Islam Rafi, Sherin Afrin Mim, Nazira Bani Opi, Dewan Fahad Chowdhury, and Md. Rejaul Korim Sadi. (2026). Predicting Student Attrition in Competitive Programming: A Large-Scale Study Integrating Survey Insights and Global Behavioral Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28618
title: Proof-of-concept Early Warning System flagging high-attrition-risk active students
description: An Early Warning System (EWS) that deploys the survey-trained Random Forest pipeline over currently active students, assigning continuous attrition risk scores (0–100%) and tiering students into High (≥67%), Medium (33–67%), and Low (<33%) risk. Applied to 22 active students, it "identified 4 students as High Risk (18%)". The flagged students all had A or A+ DSA grades, irregular upsolving habits, and no mentor support, matching the Skill-Application Paradox signature. The article treats the flags as indicators for proactive mentoring outreach, not deterministic predictions.
requirements: A trained survey-based predictive pipeline and currently active students with psychographic survey responses to score
constraints: The article states the deployment is a proof-of-concept demonstration only, with no longitudinal follow-up data available to verify whether flagged students subsequently experienced attrition
target_learners: University computer science students active in competitive programming
target_learning_goals: Sustained participation and skill development in competitive programming
examples: Deployed over 22 currently active survey respondents, categorizing 4 as High Risk (18%), 6 as Medium Risk (27%), and 12 as Low Risk (55%)
key_sources: Azuad Islam Ruhan, Golam Mostofa Naeem, Rakibul Islam Rafi, Sherin Afrin Mim, Nazira Bani Opi, Dewan Fahad Chowdhury, and Md. Rejaul Korim Sadi. (2026). Predicting Student Attrition in Competitive Programming: A Large-Scale Study Integrating Survey Insights and Global Behavioral Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28618

article_title: ProductiveMath: A Generative-AI-Powered App to Support Productive Failure Teaching
citation: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202
title: CPIG: the creative psychometric item generator framework
description: CPIG is an iterative LLM-based framework for generating and validating creativity test items for the creative problem-solving (CPS) task. It uses LLMs as "item generators" to write items, "item response generators" to create human-like solutions under baseline, demographic, or psychometric prompting profiles, and an item scorer (a roberta-base originality model) to select k high-originality items as few-shot exemplars for the next generation round. The article hypothesizes that "items with high quality should enable more creative responses and will tend to elicit better originality scores on average than those that are of lower quality," making originality a proxy for item quality. It extends automated item generation, which has focused on multiple-choice cognitive and non-cognitive items, into the creativity domain.
requirements: Items must describe sufficiently complex yet ambiguous scenarios with no canonically correct solution, and the framework requires an automated originality scoring model validated against human ratings
constraints: The framework optimizes originality only, which the authors note is just one metric for judging creative outputs; item quality depends directly on the automated evaluation, and the authors caution against using CPIG items with human participants until more extensive review
target_learners: human test takers of creativity assessments
LLM test takers used as human simulacra
target_learning_goals: measuring creative problem-solving and originality of ideas
examples: In each trial, word lists generated by gpt-3.5-turbo constrain item generation, and four selected exemplar items are included in the prompt for the next of five iterations
key_sources: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202

article_title: ProductiveMath: A Generative-AI-Powered App to Support Productive Failure Teaching
citation: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202
title: Multi-stage prompting with rule-based quality filters for LLM item generation
description: CPIG's item generation follows a multi-stage prompting pattern: a first LLM produces word lists (three names, a place, and an action) that item-generator LLMs must incorporate, which the authors say helps "maximize diversity in scenario content by using different word lists to ensure no two item generation prompts are the same." Generated scenarios then pass rule-based validity filters: a Flesch reading-ease floor of 45 with a 140-token minimum, a string blacklist targeting priming (e.g., scenarios containing "on the one hand" or "is torn between"), and a required termination string. The pattern is meant to reduce, not replace, human expert review of items.
requirements: Human experts make the final decision on which items to include in a creativity assessment; the filters only eliminate items unlikely to be valid
constraints: The authors do not claim the priming string list is comprehensive, stating only that it eliminated most priming in generated scenarios
target_learners: human test takers of creativity assessments
target_learning_goals: generating valid, diverse creative problem-solving test items
examples: Scenarios are dropped if they lack the string "I am finished with this scenario." or score below 45 on Flesch reading ease; each word list gets at most 10 generation attempts
key_sources: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202

article_title: An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
citation: Fan Ouyang, Weiqi Xu, Mutlu Cukurova. (2023). An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:39–66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09387-z
title: Complex adaptive systems theory account of CPS: multimodal, dynamic and synergistic emergence of a self-organising collaboration system
description: The article interprets CPS through complex adaptive systems theory: group members form "an adaptive, self-organizing system that has a multi-dimensional nature, synergistic relations, and a dynamic evolutionary character". CPS is multimodal (interactive, cognitive, regulative, behavioural, socio-emotional dimensions), dynamic (dsrelations change over time as groups move from communication to behaviour and back), and synergistic (coordination between communication and behaviour, most evident in the high-performing Type 2 groups). This lens breaks with causal, linear models in favour of organic, non-linear, holistic analysis.
requirements: Multimodal multi-dimensional data capturing the interdependent dimensions of collaboration over time
constraints: Studying CPS through this lens "poses significant methodological challenges to traditional statistics" used with homogeneous, unimodal data

Achieving a high-quality synergy between communication and behaviour is described as difficult; external factors such as task difficulty, group configuration, and social learning context limit all groups collaborating synergistically
target_learners: student groups in K-12 and higher education collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: understanding the emergence of adaptive self-organizing group collaboration
examples: HMM state-transition patterns showed groups evolving from communication states, to behaviour states, and back to communication, forming a self-organizing system
key_sources: Fan Ouyang, Weiqi Xu, Mutlu Cukurova. (2023). An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:39–66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09387-z

article_title: “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education
citation: Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen, Päivi Häkkinen, Pasi Tarhonen, Piia Näykki, Sanna Järvelä. (2022). “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09562-5
title: The Hesse et al. CPS framework: two first-order components, five second-order elements, and 19 third-order sub-elements used for directed content analysis
description: The study applies the ATC21S CPS framework, in which "CPS is defined as a set of elements consisting of 'social' and 'cognitive' as the first-order components". The second-order components are three social elements (participation, perspective taking, social regulation) and two cognitive elements (task regulation, knowledge building), which are "further divided into 19 specific sub-elements as third-order components". Because the framework "profoundly covers both social and cognitive elements" and specifies operational definitions, the authors judged it "suitable for the purposes of directed content analysis". The elements "can overlap and run parallel between the different stages of the process".
requirements: A condensed codebook: the article notes the framework "included a large number of code variables" that were too many for manual coding, so categories were condensed from the Hesse et al. codebook
constraints: The framework was originally developed for the targets of automated assessment of CPS skills; applying it to manual coding of group-level interaction over time is this study's extension
target_learners: small groups of learners collaborating face to face
target_learning_goals: social and cognitive elements of collaborative problem solving, including participation, perspective taking, social regulation, task regulation, and knowledge building
examples: A categorization matrix modified from the framework and codebook was used to code 26 hours of video in Atlas.ti, with deductive coding carried out three times for qualitative rigor
key_sources: Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen, Päivi Häkkinen, Pasi Tarhonen, Piia Näykki, Sanna Järvelä. (2022). “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09562-5

article_title: “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education
citation: Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen, Päivi Häkkinen, Pasi Tarhonen, Piia Näykki, Sanna Järvelä. (2022). “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09562-5
title: CPS circles: visualizations of the temporal interchange of social and cognitive states and state changes during CPS sessions
description: CPS circles are visualizations developed for this study that display, clockwise, social and cognitive state changes and their intensity during the sessions, alongside the periods when macro-script cards were discussed. "The intensity of the appearance, reflecting the number of social or cognitive sub-elements activated at a specific point, is visualized by the height of the 'ray.'" Dark gray marks social states and light gray cognitive states, giving an overview of "the alignment of CPS actions over time" across each group and task.
requirements: Timestamped, coded interaction data with calculated social and cognitive state values and inter-event state-change distances as input to the visualization
constraints: The visualizations cover the two focal CPS task sessions in this course; they were developed for this study and are interpreted alongside, not instead of, content analysis and qualitative cases
target_learners: teacher education students in small co-located collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: understanding group-level CPS enactment, including the temporal interchange of social and cognitive elements
examples: Figures 6–11 present CPS circles for Groups B, C, and D in Tasks 1 and 2, with script-card discussion periods marked in the lightest gray

Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09562-5

article_title: Creative problem solving in primary school students
citation: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823
title: The CPS model describes creative problem solving as four main elements, with the first three applied flexibly and iteratively
description: The Creative Problem Solving (CPS) model of Isaksen, Treffinger and colleagues describes creative problem solving as a set of behaviors organized into four main elements: "understanding the challenge, generating ideas, preparing for action and planning your approach". The first three elements are flexible and dynamic in ordering, so students may switch back and forth between them iteratively, while the fourth element covers planning and monitoring the process. The article applies this education-oriented model to study how primary school students solve everyday problems creatively.
requirements: Students work on an open, everyday problem situation that allows interpretation and idea generation
constraints: The model was adapted specifically for the educational context by Treffinger, Isaksen and colleagues
target_learning_goals: creative problem solving of everyday problems in science, social, and entrepreneurial domains
examples: In Study 1, 13 fourth graders thought aloud while completing a structured science problem task, and their verbalized behaviors were coded against the four CPS elements
key_sources: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823

article_title: Creative problem solving in primary school students
citation: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823
title: Four creative problem solving product indicators: fluency, originality, completeness, and practicality
description: The article treats the products of creative problem solving as ideas rated on four indicators. Fluency is the number of ideas a student generates, while "Solutions that a student ends up with after a creative problem solving process are usually regarded as creative when they are original, complete and practical". This extends classic divergent thinking scoring (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) by emphasizing usefulness: ideas should be assessed not only for quantity and originality but also for how complete and practical they are. In Study 2 these indicators were operationalized as latent factors rated via a modified Consensual Assessment Technique.
requirements: Ideas generated in response to a problem situation, with top-scoring selection to fix the number of rated ideas per student
constraints: The flexibility factor is less frequently applied in later creativity assessment because of its strong correlations with fluency
target_learning_goals: evaluating the creativity of students' problem-solving ideas
examples: In Study 2, two trained raters rated students' self-selected top-three ideas on 5-point scales for originality, completeness, and practicality, and counted fluency as the number of different ideas listed
key_sources: Van Hooijdonk, M., Mainhard, T., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Tartwijk, J. (2023). Creative problem solving in primary school students. Learning and Instruction, 88, 101823. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101823

article_title: Complex problem solving in educational contexts—Something beyond g: Concept, assessment, measurement invariance, and construct validity.
citation: Greiff, S., Wüstenberg, S., Molnár, G., Fischer, A., Funke, J., & Csapó, B. (2013, February 18). Complex Problem Solving in Educational Contexts—Something Beyond g: Concept, Assessment, Measurement Invariance, and Construct Validity. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031856
title: Two-process cognitive framework of complex problem solving: knowledge acquisition and knowledge application
description: This framework, drawn from the European CPS research tradition (Dörner, Funke), holds that "two main demands specify a problem solver's performance within the realm of CPS: knowledge acquisition and knowledge application" (Funke, 2001). Knowledge acquisition concerns building a problem representation of an unknown, dynamic system through exploration; knowledge application concerns using that representation to reach goal states. The article operationalizes the two processes as separate MicroDYN phases and tests them as distinct but correlated latent dimensions. It connects to problem-representation and problem-solution research in the Newell and Simon tradition.
requirements: Assessment must present an unknown dynamic system whose regularities can only be revealed through active exploration, since pencil-and-paper formats cannot capture interactive system behavior
constraints: The framework targets domain-general processes when solvers first face an unknown system; domain-specific knowledge becomes increasingly involved with repeated exposure and is deliberately minimized in the tasks
target_learners: high school students in Grades 5 to 11 (ages 11 to 17)
target_learning_goals: cross-curricular complex problem solving, including exploring unknown systems and applying acquired knowledge to reach goals
examples: MicroDYN implements the framework in two phases: an evaluation-free exploration phase in which solvers draw the connections between variables onscreen, and a phase in which they reach given target values on output variables
key_sources: Greiff, S., Wüstenberg, S., Molnár, G., Fischer, A., Funke, J., & Csapó, B. (2013, February 18). Complex Problem Solving in Educational Contexts—Something Beyond g: Concept, Assessment, Measurement Invariance, and Construct Validity. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031856

article_title: A Measurement Model of Microgenetic Transfer for Improving Instructional Outcomes
citation: Pavlik Jr, P. I., Yudelson, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). A Measurement Model of Microgenetic Transfer for Improving Instructional Outcomes. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0039-y
title: CPFA: a contextual performance factors analysis model of learning and transfer
description: CPFA is a mixed-effect logistic regression model that crosses source practice contexts with target performance contexts, estimating separate coefficients for learning and transfer given prior successes (gamma) and failures (rho), for a total of eight learning and transfer parameters. Unlike Q-matrix approaches, it 'explicitly assumes asymmetric (one-way) transfer may occur and does not presume any latent factors exist'. It supports a microgenetic, trial-by-trial analysis of change and can summarize complex transfer patterns 'within a small table of numbers'.
requirements: Randomized item sequences and random-effect intercepts for students and items, since without random effects 'the models estimates of learning and transfer will be confounded'
constraints: In this paper the scope was 'kept... limited to item-types and performance categories', though the mixed-effect form could include other hierarchical factors
target_learning_goals: Pre-algebra skills such as least common multiple and fraction addition
examples: Applied to two pre-algebra warm-up lessons delivered in the Carnegie Learning Bridge to Algebra tutor, each of 16 randomly selected items from sets of 24
key_sources: Pavlik Jr, P. I., Yudelson, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). A Measurement Model of Microgenetic Transfer for Improving Instructional Outcomes. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0039-y

article_title: Keep Me in the Loop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data
citation: Di Mitri, D., Schneider, J., & Drachsler, H. (2022). KeepMeInTheLoop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1093–1118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00281-z
title: CPR Tutor system architecture implementing the five-step Multimodal Pipeline with three layers
description: The CPR Tutor is a C# application collecting Kinect v2 depth-camera and Myo EMG armband data for CPR training. Its architecture "implements the five-step approach introduced by the Multimodal Pipeline" for collection, storing, annotation, processing and exploitation of multimodal data, and features Presentation, Application and Data layers. It supports offline model training and real-time exploitation with audio feedback.
requirements: Kinect v2 depth camera and Myo EMG armband sensors
annotated training data with ground-truth performance metrics from the ResusciAnne manikin SimPad
constraints: The study covered only chest compressions, not rescue ventilation, preparation, or AED use
CC segmentation in the feedback dataset differed from the manikin baseline, preventing comparison of classification results
target_learning_goals: correct chest compression technique in CPR
examples: The architecture was used to train LSTM models on expert data and deliver audio feedback in a field study at the Aachen Interdisciplinary Training Centre for Medical Education

article_title: Evaluation of the digital teacher professional development TARGET-tool for optimizing the motivational climate in secondary school physical education
citation: Weeldenburg, G., Slingerland, M., Borghouts, L. B., Kromkamp, L., van Dijk, B., van der Born, E., & Vos, S. (2024). Evaluation of the digital teacher professional development TARGET-tool for optimizing the motivational climate in secondary school physical education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10379-5
title: Digital CPD tools should align with CPD prerequisites—active teacher involvement, practice applicability, critical reflection, and iterative experimentation—to support professional growth
description: The article argues that for digital tools to be effective in continuing professional development, they should meet literature-based CPD prerequisites: being evidence-informed, facilitating active teacher involvement, addressing teachers' needs and interests, being aligned with and applicable in professional practice, stimulating critical reflection, supporting iterative cycles of experimentation and reflection within a safe environment, and focusing on student outcomes. The TARGET-tool was designed around these prerequisites, and the evaluation suggests that a tool engaging teachers as active, reflective participants can induce changes across all IMPG domains.
requirements: Tools must bridge the gap between theory and practice and provide access to scientific insights in professional practice
constraints: Successful implementation is complex and not evident; time and collaboration conditions in schools must be provided
target_learning_goals: Bridging theory and practice in teaching
examples: The TARGET-tool operationalizes these prerequisites via student scans for objective data, strategy experimentation in practice, and reflection prompts

citation: Takaria. J, Rumahlatu. D. (2016). The Effectiveness of CPS-ALM Model in Enhancing Statistical Literacy Ability and Self Concept of Elementary School Student Teacher. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: CPS-ALM: Collaborative Problem Solving assisted by literacy media, structured in five collaborative learning stages
description: CPS-ALM is a learning model combining collaborative problem solving with literacy media (e.g., graphs from a mathematics blog) to build statistical literacy and self-concept in statistics courses. The article states "There are five stages in collaborative learning amo ng others are: Engagement, Exploration, Transformation, Presentation and Reflection (Reid, 2004)", and holds that collaboration lets students with diverse mindsets complete each other and improve weaknesses while constructing creative ideas.
requirements: Group work in which students interact, argue, and cooperate, so learning results from diversity of individual opinions rather than unity
constraints: The article presents the model for statistics lecturing with elementary school student teachers in the PGSD program
target_learners: elementary school student teachers in a statistics education course
examples: The experiment group in the quasi-experiment was taught with the CPS-ALM model while the control group received expository learning

Its preparation was guided by "multiculturalism / diversity curriculum guidelines created by National council for social studies (NCSS)" and it "consists of three major topics: Basic knowledge of multicultural education, responsible behaviours and the need for multicultural education". The package contains contents to be taught as well as teachers' and students' activities, and is designed to create awareness and promote multicultural values in students.

Contains contents to be taught as well as teachers' and students' activities

article_title: The Effect of Jumping Task Based on Creative Problem Solving on Students' Problem Solving Ability
citation: Hobri, Ummah, I. K., Yuliati, N., & Dafik (2020). The Effect of Jumping Task Based on Creative Problem Solving on Students’ Problem Solving Ability. International Journal of Instruction, 13(1), 387-406. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13126a
title: Six-phase Creative Problem Solving lesson syntax (Osborn-Parnes finding sequence)
description: The article structures its CPS-based lessons with the Osborn-Parnes six-phase syntax: the Osborn -Parnes CPS process (Kandemir, 2009) is classified into six forms, namely (1) finding object, (2) finding fact, (3) finding problem, (4) finding ideas, (5) finding solution, and ( 6) finding acceptance. Each phase is given a classroom explanation in Table 1, from brainstorming goals in groups through evaluating ideas against criteria to considering real issues with new ways to solve problems creatively.
requirements: Students discuss and reach consensus on group goals in the opening phase
The teacher lists student perspectives and gives time to reflect on relevant facts
constraints: The syntax is presented as sourced from Purwati (2015) and applied here to eighth-grade mathematics with jumping or sharing tasks
target_learners: eighth-grade junior high school mathematics students
examples: Experimental classes x1 and x2 both used this CPS syntax, differing only in whether worksheets contained jumping task or sharing task exercises

article_title: Conceptual Problem Solving in High School Physics
citation: Docktor, J. L., Strand, N. E., Mestre, J. P., & Ross, B. H. (2015). Conceptual problem solving in high school physics. Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research 11, 020106. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevSTPER.11.020106
title: Conceptual Problem Solving (CPS) framework: principle, justification, plan
description: CPS is a framework for solving physics problems, not a curriculum, adapted from college strategy-writing work for high school students. It contains three parts: "Principle (the principle or concept applicable to the problem), justification (explanation of why the concept or principle is appropriate), and plan (numbered steps that provide the “recipe” for solving the problem". Students format solutions in two columns, with plan steps on the left and equations on the right, supported initially by worksheet templates and scaffolding.
requirements: Scaffolding such as headings or blank worksheet templates prompting each part when first introduced
Teachers grade or require use of the approach on homework or exams to overcome student resistance to writing
constraints: Not a curriculum; designed to be adapted to existing course materials
Writing principle-justification-plan before solving is encouraged but not required
target_learners: high school physics students in non-AP introductory mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate physics principles for problems
examples: Teachers at three schools implemented CPS flexibly: teacher A used it for advanced multistep problems, teacher B used researchers' materials for all problem solving, teacher C practiced principle and justification steps for several problems with full solutions for one or two
key_sources: Docktor, J. L., Strand, N. E., Mestre, J. P., & Ross, B. H. (2015). Conceptual problem solving in high school physics. Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research 11, 020106. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevSTPER.11.020106

article_title: Conceptual Problem Solving in High School Physics
citation: Docktor, J. L., Strand, N. E., Mestre, J. P., & Ross, B. H. (2015). Conceptual problem solving in high school physics. Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research 11, 020106. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevSTPER.11.020106
title: Two-column solution format pairing written plan steps with equations
description: A solution format in which students "carry out their plan for solving the problem by formatting their solution as two columns: A left column describing the plan step, and a right column consisting of equations or mathematics that go with each step in the plan". This pairs each conceptual planning step with its mathematical execution, making the conceptual basis of the solution visible alongside the algebra.
requirements: A written plan with numbered steps before or alongside the quantitative solution
constraints: Teacher B modified the format so students wrote plan steps directly into the left column to reduce recopying
target_learning_goals: connecting conceptual plans to mathematical procedures
examples: The sample roller-coaster problem in Fig. 2 shows plan steps such as drawing a picture and assigning symbols, writing the conservation of mechanical energy equation, and solving for final speed, each paired with its equations
key_sources: Docktor, J. L., Strand, N. E., Mestre, J. P., & Ross, B. H. (2015). Conceptual problem solving in high school physics. Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research 11, 020106. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevSTPER.11.020106

article_title: The Effects of the Classroom Performance System on Student Participation, Attendance, and Achievement
citation: Termos, M. H. (2013). The Effects of the Classroom Performance System on Student Participation, Attendance, and Achievement. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 25(1), 66-78. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/
title: Classroom Performance System (CPS) clicker technology
description: The Classroom Performance System is a low-cost radio-frequency instructional technology developed by eInstruction Corporation whose goal is "to elicit feedback or responses from a live audience in a classroom". It comprises response pads (clickers), a receiver, and software that lets instructors take attendance, deliver quizzes and surveys, record grades, generate reports, and export results. The software assigns each pad a code and creates a user profile, but displays only clicker numbers in front of the class so student anonymity is protected. In this study it delivered true/false, multiple-choice, and group work-based questions with immediate feedback and a histogram of class performance.
requirements: Requires response pads, a receiver connected to a computer via serial or USB port, and the CPS software; one receiver is enough for a classroom of about 90 to 100 students
constraints: Effectiveness depends on how the instructor uses it; depending just on the CPS questions without a change in the overall pedagogical approach may limit the effect of the system
target_learners: college students in anatomy and physiology, most of whom use English as a second language
target_learning_goals: increased participation, attendance, and achievement in lecture-based science courses
examples: In the study, approximately five true/false or multiple-choice questions of 20 to 60 seconds were delivered during each lecture, plus one to two group work-based questions lasting five to 15 minutes
key_sources: Termos, M. H. (2013). The Effects of the Classroom Performance System on Student Participation, Attendance, and Achievement. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 25(1), 66-78. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/

article_title: When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education
citation: CHENG Kai Wen. (2011). When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education. New Horizons in Education, 59(1), 106-118.
title: Treffinger, Isaksen and Dorval's three-component, six-stage Creative Problem Solving (CPS) process
description: The article describes the CPS process as a structured creativity-nurturing framework that 'mainly starts with divergent thinking and gradually end with convergent thinking.' The version adopted in this study, proposed by Treffinger, Isaksen and Dorval (1994), comprises three components — understanding the problem, generating ideas, and planning for action — and six stages: Objective-Finding, Data-Finding, Problem-Finding, Idea-Finding, Solution-Finding, and Acceptance-Finding. The author adopted this process to design the content and activities of the experimental teaching for EG1.
requirements: A well-designed method for cultivating creativity, based on the belief that creativity can be nurtured
constraints: Students unfamiliar with the process may act with confusion; the author found a 50-minute introduction was not sufficient and participants may need more guidance and supervision throughout the process
target_learners: first-year university students in a hotel management program
examples: EG1 students completed 'creative problem-solving learning sheets' under CPS process during group discussion, with the teacher observing to ensure discussion proceeded according to CPS process.
key_sources: CHENG Kai Wen. (2011). When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education. New Horizons in Education, 59(1), 106-118. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ955493

article_title: Midwest Child-Parent Center (CPC) PreK-3rd Grade School Reform Model: Impacts on Child and Family Outcomes over Time
citation: Erika Gaylor, Donna Spiker, Xin Wei, Erin Lease, Arthur Reynolds. (2015). Midwest Child-Parent Center (CPC) PreK-3rd Grade School Reform Model: Impacts on Child and Family Outcomes Over Time. SREE Spring 2015 Conference.
title: CPC Expansion Program elements: collaborative leadership team, effective learning experiences, menu-based parent involvement, continuity and stability, aligned curriculum, and professional development system
description: The CPC Expansion Program provides continuous education and family support services from Preschool to Third Grade to schools serving large percentages of low-income children. The program has the following elements: (1) collaborative leadership team of Head Teacher, Parent Resource Teacher, and School-Community Representative under the supervision of the Principal; (2) effective learning experiences (e.g., small classes, intensive learning opportunities); (3) menu-based system of parent involvement and engagement; (4) continuity and stability; (5) aligned curriculum; and (6) professional development system of coaching and on-line modules.
requirements: The foundation of the program is the leadership team of the Head Teacher, Parent Resource Teacher, and School-Community Representative who partner with the principal to create a shared vision and structure of implementation.
constraints: The program is being implemented in 4 school districts in the Midwest using a collaborative implementation approach to promote sustainability.
target_learners: low-income children at-risk for poor school achievement
examples: In 2012-2013, over 2,300 PreK children enrolled in the program across the 26 schools. At the end of kindergarten over 4,000 children were served.
key_sources: Erika Gaylor, Donna Spiker, Xin Wei, Erin Lease, Arthur Reynolds. (2015). Midwest Child-Parent Center (CPC) PreK-3rd Grade School Reform Model: Impacts on Child and Family Outcomes Over Time. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562345

article_title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practice Determinants of Wound Management Among Nurses and Midwives in Central Ethiopia: A Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Lonsako Deginet Tesfaye, Sugebo Ermias Sigebo. (2026). Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practice Determinants of Wound Management Among Nurses and Midwives in Central Ethiopia: A Cross‐Sectional Study. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.71073
title: Prioritize structured continuous professional development over pre-service academic upgrades to close wound-care knowledge gaps
description: The article concludes that because formal in-service training was the sole independent predictor of good knowledge while degrees conferred no advantage, hospitals should establish "structured, mandatory wound care workshops prioritizing aseptic technique, dressing selection, and infection control." It emphasizes CPD as the operational priority over basic pre-service academic upgrades.
requirements: Hospital management commitment to establish structured, mandatory wound care workshops
constraints: Findings derive from a single tertiary institution and may have limited generalizability to lower-tier facilities
target_learners: Registered nurses and midwives in tertiary referral hospitals
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based wound-care knowledge including aseptic technique, dressing selection, and infection control
examples: The hospital management should establish structured, mandatory wound care workshops prioritizing aseptic technique, dressing selection, and infection control.
key_sources: Lonsako Deginet Tesfaye, Sugebo Ermias Sigebo. (2026). Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practice Determinants of Wound Management Among Nurses and Midwives in Central Ethiopia: A Cross‐Sectional Study. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.71073

article_title: First Experience With Using a Simulator in Teaching Physiology of the Cardiovascular System.
citation: Mazgutova N, Mokra D, Calkovska A, Plevkova J, Biringerova Z, Mokry J. (2026). Teaching Physiology-First Experience With Using a Simulator in Teaching Physiology of the Cardiovascular System. Physiological Research. https://doi.org/10.33549/physiolres.935831
title: CPS Harvey cardiopulmonary auscultation patient simulator
description: The CPS Harvey is a moderate-fidelity, life-size patient simulator that realistically simulates various cardiac findings and respiratory murmurs. Students selected physiological and pathological auscultation findings (e.g. systolic, diastolic, continuous murmurs) in random order from its menu, and used it to train heart auscultation and blood pressure measurement under normotensive, hypotensive and hypertensive conditions.
requirements: Used in small groups of 4-8 students with instructor/demonstrator support
Accompanying programs and case notes provided for pre-class self-study
constraints: Session duration limited to 90 minutes due to space and time limitations in the simulation center
target_learning_goals: Recognition of physiological and pathological heart sounds and murmurs
examples: Students auscultated the mitral, tricuspid, aortic and pulmonary valve areas on the mannequin after practicing on peers in pairs
key_sources: Mazgutova N, Mokra D, Calkovska A, Plevkova J, Biringerova Z, Mokry J. (2026). Teaching Physiology-First Experience With Using a Simulator in Teaching Physiology of the Cardiovascular System. Physiological Research. https://doi.org/10.33549/physiolres.935831

citation: Kamphausen Anne, Pilz Maximilian, Baumgärtel Matthias, Kubitz Jens Christian, Engelen Christian. (2026). Effect of an app-guided advanced cardiac life support algorithm on teamwork, non-technical skills, and workload in simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest: a randomized controlled feasibility trial. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-026-01673-7
title: CPR Team Leader app: tablet-based ALS algorithm cognitive aid
description: The 'CPR Team Leader' application (Version 1.0.9; Alphabet Medical GmbH) is a Class I medical device designed to support resuscitation teams in adhering to ALS algorithms. "Beyond displaying the relevant algorithm branch, the app provides integrated timers for rhythm-check and medication intervals, audible and visual reminders, and input fields for documenting administered medications and defibrillations." It was operated by the team leader during intervention scenarios.
requirements: Structured instruction and online training on app use prior to deployment, as provided to all hospital departments
constraints: Extent and pattern of app use during scenarios varied between participants and was not standardized or quantified
target_learners: In-hospital resuscitation team leaders and teams
target_learning_goals: Adherence to advanced life support algorithms during cardiac arrest
examples: Used on an Apple tablet by team leaders during simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest scenarios following the 2021 German Resuscitation Council ALS algorithm

Effect of an app-guided advanced cardiac life support algorithm on teamwork, non-technical skills, and workload in simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest: a randomized controlled feasibility trial. article_title: Enhancing professional adaptability and clinical soft skills of new clinical pharmacists through a pre-training model in China: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Wang Tianlin, Liang Jinmei, Chen Li, Li Shu, Zhu Man, Cai Yun, Chen Mengli. (2025). Enhancing professional adaptability and clinical soft skills of new clinical pharmacists through a pre-training model in China: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07951-9
title: CPOAL: a two-stage, three-month pre-training program for newly recruited pharmacists without clinical pharmacy backgrounds
description: The Clinical Pharmacist Occupational Adaptive Learning (CPOAL) program is a three-month pre-training delivered before China's one-year standardized clinical pharmacist training. Its first stage is two weeks of job awareness training covering "the daily work schedule, personnel management system, basic work content, skill requirements (professional and communication skills), and assessment criteria". The second stage teaches basic clinical diagnosis and treatment processes and common medical software, with clinical pharmacist instructors covering prescription review, patient monitoring, medication education, and pharmacy consultation, and clinician instructors teaching ward rounds, history taking, diagnosis, and follow-up, via centralised lectures and on-site teaching in general medicine wards.
requirements: Senior experts in clinical pharmacy or clinical medicine as instructors
Access to affiliated hospital wards and medical software for on-site teaching
Delivery before the one-year standardized training
constraints: Developed for the Chinese pathway in which NRPs are graduates of basic pharmacy programs without clinical medicine training or internships; the article states its design did not draw on training models for nurses, physicians, or clinical pharmacists from other countries
target_learners: Newly recruited pharmacists without a clinical pharmacy academic background
target_learning_goals: Clinical soft skills including communication, adaptability, and clinical reasoning
examples: In the trial, 10 NRPs received the three-month program before one-year standardized training while 10 controls went directly into standardized training
key_sources: Wang Tianlin, Liang Jinmei, Chen Li, Li Shu, Zhu Man, Cai Yun, Chen Mengli. (2025). Enhancing professional adaptability and clinical soft skills of new clinical pharmacists through a pre-training model in China: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07951-9

article_title: CPADS-30: Mastering the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation.
citation: Ford James S. MD, MAS, Malhotra Atul MD, Pearce Alex K. MD, Wardi Gabriel MD, MPH. (2025). CPADS-30: Mastering the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation. The American journal of emergency medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajem.2025.06.056
title: CPADS-30 mnemonic for the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation
description: CPADS-30 is a five-item mnemonic for code leaders covering Chest compressions, Pads (defibrillator), Access (IV/IO), Drugs, and Scribe assignment, to be prioritized within the first 30 seconds. The authors describe it as a "simplified mnemonic designed to facilitate memory recall and facilitate task delegation in the first 30 s of cardiac arrest resuscitation" that complements the complete ACLS algorithm. It was developed by four clinical content experts through literature review and consensus ranking.
requirements: IV/IO access must be established before medications can be delivered, so the D task depends on the A task
a team member must be available to fulfill the scribe role
constraints: not intended to be a comprehensive roadmap for cardiac resuscitation
not intended for use in children, as pediatric cardiac arrest resuscitations have special considerations
not yet empirically tested; future studies will assess process and outcome measures
target_learners: code leaders including trainees and early-career providers
pre-hospital providers and clinicians in all hospital settings
target_learning_goals: rapid recall and delegation of critical early resuscitation tasks in the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest
examples: Table 1 assigns each letter a task and explanation: C assigns first and second CPR rounds, P places pads and hooks up the defibrillator, A establishes IV/IO access, D pulls and readies medications, S handles documentation and time keeping
key_sources: Ford James S. MD, MAS, Malhotra Atul MD, Pearce Alex K. MD, Wardi Gabriel MD, MPH. (2025). CPADS-30: Mastering the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation. The American journal of emergency medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajem.2025.06.056

article_title: Advancing healthcare practice and education via data sharing: demonstrating the utility of open data by training an artificial intelligence model to assess cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills.
citation: Constable, M. D., Zhang, F. X., Conner, T., Monk, D., Rajsic, J., Ford, C., Park, L. J., Platt, A., Porteous, D., Grierson, L., & Shum, H. P. H. (2025). Advancing healthcare practice and education via data sharing: demonstrating the utility of open data by training an artificial intelligence model to assess cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 30(1), 15-35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10369-5
title: CPR skills performance video database hosted at the UK Data Service ReShare Repository
description: A shared dataset of CPR performances of varied quality, collected for this research and hosted at UK Data Service's ReShare Repository. The article states it "contains videos from 40 participants recorded from 6 different angles, allowing for 3D reconstruction for movement analysis", accompanied by expert quality ratings from 2 raters, self-reported confidence and frequency of performing CPR, and participant demographics. Access is safeguarded: researchers email the data controller stating their status and intention, and agree to repository terms restricting use to research or learning purposes and maintaining participant confidentiality.
requirements: Users must register, agree to the repository's terms and conditions, use the data only for research or learning purposes, and maintain participant confidentiality.
constraints: Participants who did not consent to use outside the research team are not included; participants could elect to share only videos or only evaluations.
examples: 53 participants were recorded on three recruitment days across varied expertise levels; participants performed 4 sets of 30 chest compressions recorded by 6 Go-Pro cameras with a checkerboard landmark for calibration.

Advancing healthcare practice and education via data sharing: demonstrating the utility of open data by training an artificial intelligence model to assess cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills. article_title: An observer tool to enhance learning of medical students during simulation training of cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Goulamhoussen Ammar, Havard Caroline, Gille Benoit, François Bob, Benhamou Dan, Blanié Antonia. (2024). An observer tool to enhance learning of medical students during simulation training of cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05658-x
title: Observer tool: a 25-item checklist for observers of CPR simulation
description: The observer tool (OT) is a checklist "summarizing CPR skills and step-by-step actions" that observers fill in (observed/incompletely/not observed) for each item and each observation sequence. It was "designed by expert investigators in accordance with the 2021 recommendations of the European Resuscitation Council", tested and validated by experts, and totalled 25 items, with 7, 13, 20 and 25 items active as successive teaching steps were added.
requirements: Students in the observer role must fill in the form for each of the 25 items during each observation sequence
The checklist must reflect current resuscitation recommendations (2021 European Resuscitation Council)
constraints: The authors note that no guidelines on how to create and present an OT are available, and it remains possible that their OT was not easy to use
target_learners: second-year medical students in basic life support training
target_learning_goals: recognition of unconsciousness and absence of breathing
examples: In the trial, OT+ students filled out the form as observers while dyads practised five incremental BLS steps on a Resusci Anne Q-CPR mannequin with real-time SkillReporter feedback

article_title: Evaluating the impact of continuing professional development courses on physician behavioral intention: a pre-post study with follow-up at six months.
citation: Bakwa Kanyinga Felly, Gogovor Amédé, Dofara Suélène Georgina, Gadio Souleymane, Tremblay Martin, Daniel Sam J., Rivest Louis-Paul, Légaré France. (2023). Evaluating the impact of continuing professional development courses on physician behavioral intention: a pre-post study with follow-up at six months. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04597-3
title: CPD-REACTION: a validated 12-item questionnaire measuring intention and psychosocial factors influencing intention after CPD activities
description: CPD-REACTION is a validated questionnaire based on socio-cognitive theories for evaluating the impact of CPD activities on health professionals' intention to adopt targeted behaviors. "Twelve items evaluate intention and factors associated with it", with construct scores on a Likert-type scale from 1 (low) to 7 (high); "The Cronbach's alpha coefficient ranges from 0.77 to 0.85". In this study the questionnaire was adapted to the behavior-change targets of each of the nine courses and administered before, immediately after, and in a six-month behavior-change form.
requirements: Adaptation of the questionnaire items to the specific behavior-change targets of each CPD course
constraints: The article notes there is no benchmark score signaling a statistically significant higher intention; validation studies show highest scores exceed the range mean (3.5) and tend toward the maximum of 7
target_learning_goals: evaluating impact of CPD activities on intention to adopt targeted behaviors
examples: Participants completed CPD-REACTION online on the FMSQ MÉDUSE platform one week before courses, immediately afterwards, and a self-reported behavior-change questionnaire six months later.
key_sources: Bakwa Kanyinga Felly, Gogovor Amédé, Dofara Suélène Georgina, Gadio Souleymane, Tremblay Martin, Daniel Sam J., Rivest Louis-Paul, Légaré France. (2023). Evaluating the impact of continuing professional development courses on physician behavioral intention: a pre-post study with follow-up at six months. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04597-3

article_title: Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum.
citation: Han Sang Yun, Lee Seung-Hee, Chae Han. (2022). Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03398-4
title: Two-day Clinical Performance Test combining CPX, OSCE, acupuncture needling, and medical herb assessment
description: The Clinical Performance Test (CPT) evaluates clinical competency after 25 weeks of clinical education. "One set of the test for six student examinees is composed of CPX (3 items, 10 min/item), OSCE (6 items, 5 min/item), acupuncture point location, and placing needles (2 items, 7 min/item), and preparation and processing of medical herbs (1 item, 10 min/item)". Students scoring below 60 must retake and pass the test the following year.
requirements: Ten test rooms with assigned academic staff evaluators, checklists distributed in advance via the guidebooks, and item point values ranging from 10 to 24
constraints: The article states 5 and 10 minutes are "uniformly" allocated to OSCE and CPX modules "regardless of subject, complexity, and difficulty", which the authors say should be rearranged
target_learners: final-year students of traditional Korean medicine
target_learning_goals: comprehensive clinical competency and proficiency in skills, techniques and procedures
examples: Acupuncture competence is tested with subgroup members or a manikin as patients, scored on point location, needling depth and angle, and Clean Needle Technique

article_title: The Effect of Educational Intervention on the Improvement of Nontechnical Skills in Circulating Nurses.
citation: Kalantari Reza, Zamanian Zahra, Hasanshahi Mehdi, Faghihi Seyed Aliakbar, Jamali Jamshid, Niakan Hadi. (2021). The Effect of Educational Intervention on the Improvement of Nontechnical Skills in Circulating Nurses. BioMed Research International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2021/5856730
title: CPLINTS observational tool for circulating nurses' nontechnical skills
description: The circulating practitioners' list of nontechnical skills (CPLINTS) is a valid and reliable observational tool containing 43 observable behaviors grouped into five dimensions: task management, teamwork, situational awareness, communication, and leadership. Each item is scored from zero (necessary but not observed) to four (excellent), with a not-applicable option, and mean scores can be calculated per dimension. The study used it to rate nurses before and eight weeks after training, with an observer with seven years of experience who remained silent during surgeries.
requirements: Requires an experienced observer who does not disrupt the surgical team's activities during data collection
constraints: Some behaviors carry a not-applicable option because they are not needed during every surgery
target_learning_goals: assessment of nontechnical skills: task management, teamwork, situational awareness, communication, leadership
examples: Used to rate 300 circulating nurses before and eight weeks after a face-to-face educational intervention

article_title: Shorter training intervals increase high school students' awareness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a questionnaire study.
citation: Tang Hong-mei, Wu Xiao, Jin Yin, Jin Yi-qing, Wang Zi-jun, Luo Jin-yan, Hu Yan-qi, Jin Ting, Shang Moses, Chang Qing, Wang Fei. (2020). Shorter training intervals increase high school students’ awareness of cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a questionnaire study. Journal of International Medical Research. https://doi.org/10.1177/0300060519897692
title: CPR training for students should combine theoretical instruction with hands-on practice, since theory-only training leaves students unable to respond independently
description: The article states that in China "Most first aid training … places a strong emphasis on theoretical training rather than practicing the relevant techniques", meaning students may not handle sudden emergencies independently. It concludes more effective training needs "high-quality lessons that include both theoretical and practical training". This principle generalizes that recommendation for school-based first-aid education.
requirements: Access to practical skill-practice sessions, not only lectures; the article also notes regular skill consolidation training is needed.
constraints: The article notes its questionnaire covered broad CPR knowledge while public guidelines focus mainly on chest compression, and future work should target chest-compression theory and skills.
target_learning_goals: acquisition of practical CPR and basic life support skills
examples: The study's own context: 88.1% of students had attended training yet only 7.7% qualified, which the authors attribute partly to theory-dominant, short-term training formats.

article_title: A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD.
citation: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010
title: Transformation of individual's professional practice through CPD (Theory 1)
description: The first transformation theory holds that work-based CPD built on learner-driven assessment, self-awareness, and facilitated reflection within a supportive organization enhances role clarity, role development opportunities, and engagement with meaningful change. The article states that "Work based CPD built on learner driven assessment and self-awareness within a supportive organization and facilitated reflection enhances role clarity, opportunities for role development and engagement with meaningful change." Contextual factors include opportunities for work-based CPD, a culture of inquiry and learning, and supportive organizations valuing work-based learning.
requirements: Work-based CPD opportunities (C1), a culture of inquiry, learning and implementation (C2), and supportive organizations that value work-based learning and development (C3).
constraints: The theory represents a theoretical inference from realist synthesis CMO analysis, not an outcome-measured experimental result.
target_learners: NHS staff undertaking postgraduate skills development programs
target_learning_goals: Person-centred, safe and effective care practice
key_sources: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010

article_title: A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD.
citation: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010
title: Transformation of skills to meet society's changing healthcare needs (Theory 2)
description: The second transformation theory posits that assessments of gaps in systems and team skills inform CPD for transforming skills to match society's changing healthcare needs. The article states: "Assessments for gaps in systems and team skills inform CPD for transforming skills to match society's changing healthcare needs." It further posits that transforming skills impacts service user experiences, team effectiveness, career progression opportunities, and organizational partnerships. Contextual factors include a focus on team competences and effectiveness rather than just the individual.
requirements: A focus on team competences and effectiveness rather than just the individual (C4), value for money in the use of human resources (C5), and staff adaptability and flexibility in contemporary healthcare (C6).
constraints: The theory rests on the supposition that no one person can deliver all the competences and skills required to support effective healthcare, framed as a theoretical proposition rather than a measured finding.
target_learning_goals: Continuity and consistency of service user experience
key_sources: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010

article_title: A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD.
citation: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010
title: Transformation of knowledge to enable knowledge translation (Theory 3)
description: The third transformation theory conceptualizes knowledge translation as a process of analyzing, sharing and ethically applying knowledge for safe, person-centred and effective care. The article states that "Effective transformation of knowledge generates knowledge rich cultures and active contribution to practice development, innovation and creativity." Mechanisms operate at three levels: everyday decisions blending different knowledge types, facilitation skillsets enabling active inquiry and evaluation across workplace teams, and developing practical and theoretical knowledge of leadership, facilitation, evaluation and cultural aspects influencing knowledge translation.
requirements: Engaging with and using different types of knowledge in everyday practice (C7), and active sharing of knowledge in the workplace (C8).
constraints: The three-level mechanism framework reflects the authors' realist synthesis interpretation of how knowledge translation outcomes arise, not a tested hierarchical model.
target_learning_goals: Knowledge used in and developed from practice

article_title: A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD.
citation: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010
title: Transformation of workplace culture to implement organizational values and purpose (Theory 4)
description: The fourth transformation theory focuses on CPD that addresses the immediate workplace culture and implementation of shared values across the organization and the health economy. The article states: "Organizations that are ready to change promote development and implementation of shared values to enhance patient experiences, team cohesiveness, effectiveness in workplace cultures and organizational leadership." Contextual factors include explicit shared values and purposes and organizational readiness to change, with mechanisms including developing shared values, facilitating implementation through feedback and critical reflection, and evaluating experiences of shared values.
requirements: Explicit shared values and purposes (C5) and organizational readiness to change (C6) as contextual preconditions.
constraints: The theory acknowledges the need for an organization that upholds change with plans for ongoing improvements and the capacity to maintain the change; outcomes are theoretically inferred rather than measured.
target_learning_goals: Sustained person-centred, safe and effective workplace culture
Improved service user and provider experiences

article_title: A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD.
citation: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010
title: CPD effectiveness evaluation should encompass stakeholder interests rather than rely solely on outcome-based measures
description: The article argues that using an outcome-based approach alone to assess CPD effectiveness is a narrow way of understanding impact, because it "does not take into account the numerous factors that may influence practitioners' CPD activity." CPD evaluations ought to encompass stakeholders' interests in practitioners' CPD activity to answer the key concern of 'who is CPD effective for?' Effectiveness should be understood as holistic authentic learning and fitness to practice, which may exceed the capacity for quantitative measures.
requirements: Comprehensive organizational strategy for evaluation enabling measurement of outcomes, performance, and return on investment in training.
constraints: Practitioners themselves are often unable to articulate the impact of their CPD activity, undermining confidence in its value.
target_learning_goals: Understanding for whom CPD is effective
