article_title: A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD.
citation: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010
title: Transformation theories contextualize CPD drivers across individual, team, organizational and service/society levels
description: The article's theoretical framework organizes effective CPD as a pattern of changes operating across multiple levels. "A noticeable change illustrates improvements at the individual, team, organizational and service/society levels, reflective of the underlying purpose for the practitioner's CPD activity." For example, a practitioner's improved dementia assessment skill may lead to improved team efficiency, lower service delivery costs, and patient experience of seamless care. The framework holds that transformation areas are interdependent but some may require focus before others to achieve full workplace benefit.
requirements: The workplace functioning as the main resource for learning and development.
constraints: The areas for CPD transformation are interdependent but sequencing may be needed — some may require focus before others.
examples: A practitioner's improved skill in assessment and diagnosis of dementia leading to improved team efficiency, lower service delivery costs and patient experience of seamless care
key_sources: Manley K., Martin A., Jackson C., Wright T. (2018). A realist synthesis of effective continuing professional development (CPD): A case study of healthcare practitioners' CPD. Nurse Education Today. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2018.07.010

article_title: Using a Teaching Intervention and Calibrated Peer Review™ Diagnostics to Improve Visual Communication Skills.
citation: Saterbak Ann, Moturu Anoosha, Volz Tracy. (2018). Using a Teaching Intervention and Calibrated Peer Review™ Diagnostics to Improve Visual Communication Skills. Annals of Biomedical Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10439-017-1946-x
title: Calibrated Peer Review™ (CPR) as a formative-assessment and diagnostics tool for poster assignments
description: Calibrated Peer Review™ (CPR) is an asynchronous, anonymous electronic peer-review system in which students "upload their poster drafts in the Text Entry stage", rate three instructor-selected and instructor-rated sample posters in the Calibration stage, review three peers' texts, and complete a Self-Assessment stage. In BIOE 342, Rice University's bioengineering department used CPR "as a mechanism for formative assessment": students receive credit for critiques, but poster grades are determined by the instructor. CPR diagnostics revealed that students were skilled at evaluating lower-order cognitive tasks such as formatting but "performed poorly on higher-order cognitive tasks such as analysis, synthesis, and evaluation".
requirements: Students must complete the Text Entry, Calibration, Review, and Self-Assessment stages; ratings of sample posters must fall within a prescribed standard deviation before entering the Review stage
constraints: The article states that two of 15 control comparisons (Statements 12 and 13 for RQ1) returned significant results without convergence, meaning peer evaluations got worse relative to the instructor after the intervention
target_learners: Junior-level biomedical engineering undergraduates in a tissue culture laboratory course
target_learning_goals: Develop high quality graphs and tables that represent experimental data
Correctly interpret and clearly summarize the experimental results
examples: Rice University's bioengineering department integrated CPR with a poster assignment in BIOE 342, a tissue culture laboratory course, to diagnose student learning gaps in visual communication skills and to measure changes after an active learning intervention
key_sources: Saterbak Ann, Moturu Anoosha, Volz Tracy. (2018). Using a Teaching Intervention and Calibrated Peer Review™ Diagnostics to Improve Visual Communication Skills. Annals of Biomedical Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10439-017-1946-x

article_title: Scaling and Sustaining Effective Early Childhood Programs Through School-Family-University Collaboration.
citation: Reynolds Arthur J., Hayakawa Momoko, Ou Suh-Ruu, Mondi Christina F., Englund Michelle M., Candee Allyson J., Smerillo Nicole E. (2017). Scaling and Sustaining Effective Early Childhood Programs Through School-Family-University Collaboration. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12901
title: School-family-university collaboration model based on shared ownership, committed resources, and progress monitoring for improvement
description: The article frames CPC-P3 as a school reform model grounded in a collaboration model with three major principles. In "shared ownership", partners have equal responsibility to plan, implement, manage, and improve the program rather than adopting an externally developed model unmodified. In "committed resources", each partner makes key investments of "time, financial capital, and physical space". "Progress monitoring for improvement" is described as ongoing formative evaluation essential for continuous improvement, using implementation-fidelity data shared among partners.
requirements: Each partner must make key investments necessary for effective implementation, including time, financial capital, and physical space.
constraints: The article notes externally developed programs often lack sufficiently developed shared ownership, which reduces organizational commitment to scaling.
target_learners: Children ages 3 to 9 in preschool through third grade
target_learning_goals: School readiness and early school achievement
examples: Principals who contributed at least 25% of the added cost of full-day classrooms had the remainder matched by HCRC, supporting shared ownership and committed resources.
key_sources: Reynolds Arthur J., Hayakawa Momoko, Ou Suh-Ruu, Mondi Christina F., Englund Michelle M., Candee Allyson J., Smerillo Nicole E. (2017). Scaling and Sustaining Effective Early Childhood Programs Through School-Family-University Collaboration. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12901

article_title: Scaling and Sustaining Effective Early Childhood Programs Through School-Family-University Collaboration.
citation: Reynolds Arthur J., Hayakawa Momoko, Ou Suh-Ruu, Mondi Christina F., Englund Michelle M., Candee Allyson J., Smerillo Nicole E. (2017). Scaling and Sustaining Effective Early Childhood Programs Through School-Family-University Collaboration. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12901
title: CPC-P3 six core elements of the Midwest Child-Parent Center Expansion program
description: Each CPC-P3 site implements a set of six core elements following program guidelines in the manual: a collaborative leadership team run by the Head Teacher with the principal; effective learning experiences through small classes and full-day preschool and kindergarten (classes limited to 17 in preschool and 25 in K-3 with assistants); an aligned curriculum updated annually; parent involvement and engagement via menu-based services; a professional development system with online modules and on-site follow-up; and continuity and stability of services from preschool to third grade.
requirements: Sites implement the elements following the program guidelines and requirements specified in the manual (HCRC, 2012; Reynolds et al., 2016).
constraints: Table 1 identifies major barriers per element, including maintaining small classes, across-grade communication, engaging hard-to-reach families, time to review teaching practices, and student mobility.
target_learners: Low-income children ages 3 to 9 and their families in preschool through third grade
examples: Twenty-three full-day classrooms were opened in fall 2012 across participating schools.
Parent resource rooms host events, and the SCR conducts home visits and mobilizes resources for families.
